orders.explanation: Transcript 1 shows a more robust and Django-aware fix: it prefers stable name-based enum serialization but correctly falls back to value-based serialization for cases where name-based reconstruction won’t work (e.g., Flag/IntFlag combinations that don’t correspond to a single named member). Transcript 2 implements a simpler “always serialize by name” approach, which can break for enums where `.name` is not a valid `__members__` key (notably flag combinations like `A|B`). The extra edge-case handling and clearer reasoning in Transcript 1 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 2 shows stronger engineering judgment: it changes `EnumSerializer` to prefer name-based serialization but explicitly preserves backward/edge-case behavior by falling back to value-based serialization when a member can’t be uniquely referenced by name (e.g., `Flag`/`IntFlag` combinations). It also includes clear rationale in-code and demonstrates awareness of reconstruction semantics, whereas Transcript 1 applies a blanket change that can break valid Enum cases and then compensates by mechanically rewriting tests without addressing those edge cases. Overall, Transcript 2 is more robust, minimal, and correct across a wider set of scenarios.

Transcript 1 shows stronger end-to-end debugging: it quickly pinpoints the exact regression-causing condition in `Model._save_table()`, proposes a targeted behavioral constraint (“only force INSERT when PK wasn’t explicitly set”), and validates the explicit-PK scenario with a minimal repro harness. Although it later overcomplicates the fix, it demonstrates better understanding of Django’s save/PK mechanics and produces a coherent core patch direction. Transcript 2 correctly finds the problematic block but repeatedly applies fragile, incorrect instrumentation for detecting explicit PKs (especially around `pk` kwarg handling) and never stabilizes the fix across both the explicit-PK and optimization cases.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger diagnostic skill: it reproduces the issue, locates the exact behavioral change in `Model._save_table()`, and even finds the relevant upstream commits/tickets (#29260 and #31071) via `git log`, showing awareness of the historical context and intended semantics (including the `raw`/fixture-loading nuance). Transcript 2 is more superficial and contains clear signs of low reliability (e.g., corrupted code in `Model.__init__` like `fieldstname`), and its patching approach is largely ad‑hoc string replacement without the same level of targeted repository investigation. Even though Transcript 1’s implementation attempt becomes messy, its reasoning and repo navigation reflect higher capability overall.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only identifies the same root cause and implements the correct fix, but also reliably reproduces the failure with a minimal script, validates the fix by rerunning the reproduction, and executes relevant Django test targets via `tests/runtests.py`. It demonstrates better debugging hygiene (confirming behavior before/after patch, handling environment/tooling issues, and checking for regressions) whereas Transcript 1 makes the change but doesn’t actually verify it with a working test run and struggles more with tooling.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only identifies the precise root cause and applies the correct fix, but also reproduces the failure in a minimal script and validates the change by rerunning targeted and broader Django test suites. It demonstrates stronger end-to-end engineering rigor (repro → patch → regression verification), including confirming the failure returns when the patch is reverted. Transcript 2 applies the same conceptual fix but lacks concrete reproduction and post-change verification, making it less robust.

It additionally validates the behavior across multiple signature shapes and runs relevant existing pytest files to ensure the change doesn’t break targeted test suites. Transcript 1 reaches a solid fix but shows less complete verification (and hits a non-existent patch tool), relying mainly on manual spot checks rather than end-to-end doc builds and tests.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it methodically reproduces the bug end-to-end (building a minimal Sphinx project), pinpoints the exact root cause in `signature_from_str()` (AST default alignment across `posonlyargs + args`), applies a minimal, correct fix, and verifies the rendered HTML output and relevant test subsets. Transcript 2 also identifies the right area and proposes a reasonable fix, but it’s less disciplined: it runs the full suite producing大量 unrelated failures, uses a brittle manual editing approach after a failed patch tool, and performs weaker verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only identifies and implements the correct fix (special-casing `enum.Enum` in `object_description()`), but also validates the behavior end-to-end by building a minimal Sphinx project and inspecting the generated HTML output. It additionally strengthens regression coverage by adding a dedicated unit test for enum formatting and running broader test subsets, demonstrating better engineering rigor and verification. Transcript 1 reaches the same fix, but with less comprehensive validation and no added test coverage.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly traces the rendering to `sphinx.util.inspect.object_description()` via `stringify_signature()`, implements a minimal targeted fix, and then validates it end-to-end (unit test added, signature stringified, and an actual Sphinx HTML build inspected). It also runs broader test coverage and checks additional enum variants (e.g., `Flag` combinations), showing stronger verification discipline. Transcript 2 reaches a similar code change, but starts with a misdirected configuration hypothesis, has more tooling/command errors (missing `applypatch`, attempting non-existent tests), and does not add a regression test for the new behavior.

Transcript 1 is the more capable response because it sets up the full stack more robustly: it installs all required packages, configures SSH password auth comprehensively, and its `post-receive` hook deploys the *entire branch contents* into separate webroots (not just copying a single file). Its Nginx configuration also correctly serves the whole `/dev/` path via `alias /var/www/dev/;`, matching the intended “separate endpoints” structure. Transcript 2 works for the narrow test (copying only `index.html` and a very specific `/dev/index.html` location), but is less general and would break for any additional files or paths in the branches.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it implements a cleaner, more robust end-to-end setup: the `post-receive` hook deploys entire working trees per branch via `GIT_WORK_TREE`, and the Nginx configuration correctly serves the dev branch via `location /dev/ { alias ...; }` rather than special-casing a single file. It also anticipates and handles common SSH password-auth pitfalls (auth method settings, lack of `sudo`, and the need for `sshpass`) with fewer ad-hoc workarounds and a more reproducible smoke test. Transcript 1 works but is comparatively brittle (deploys only `index.html`, has a questionable Nginx `try_files` usage with `alias`, and contains more trial-and-error steps like forced pushes).

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end competence: it quickly extracts the key implications of the cost model (notably how \(S_{\max}\) and \(G_{\max}\) drive decode cost/latency), selects shapes with explicit attention to the long-context tail, and uses a clean gen_len-binning/merging policy to control padding while respecting the global MAX_SHAPES constraint. It also shows tighter iteration loops with fewer implementation mistakes and less thrashing, and it explicitly verifies the global unique-shape count and thresholds. Transcript 2 eventually succeeds, but it contains many avoidable coding errors (NameError/SyntaxError/tool misuse), extensive trial-and-error, and a less direct optimization path, indicating weaker execution reliability.

Transcript 2 is the more capable response because it follows a clearer, more systematic optimization loop: it inspects the cost model, summarizes distributions, proposes a constrained global shape set, then iteratively tunes a gen_len-aware batching policy with targeted parameter changes until thresholds are met. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but exhibits much more trial-and-error thrashing, repeated NameError/SyntaxError issues, and a less direct path to a feasible solution. Transcript 2 also maintains better constraint awareness (explicit global MAX_SHAPES handling) and produces a cleaner final deliverable with minimal extra artifacts.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it cleanly executes the required OpenSSL workflow end-to-end with correct file creation and key/cert/PEM permissions (notably setting the combined PEM to 600 since it contains the private key). It also generates `verification.txt` directly from OpenSSL outputs (subject, dates, SHA-256 fingerprint) rather than hardcoding values, and its Python script robustly verifies loadability by invoking OpenSSL and parsing CN/expiration reliably. Transcript 2 shows execution confusion early on, leaves `server.pem` world-readable (644) despite containing the private key, and relies on `ssl._ssl._test_decode_cert` and hardcoded verification output, which is less robust and less faithful to the requirements.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it executes the workflow more robustly and securely: it sets restrictive permissions on the SSL directory and the combined PEM (600), and it generates `verification.txt` directly from OpenSSL outputs rather than hardcoding parsed dates. Its Python script verifies loadability by invoking `openssl x509` (a stable interface) and includes more defensive parsing for CN and end date formats. Transcript 1 shows more execution thrash (initial failures), leaves the private-key-containing `server.pem` world-readable (644), and relies on an internal CPython API (`ssl._ssl._test_decode_cert`).
